answer: A deposit-backed identity registry makes a sybil attack expensive: every agent must lock a refundable bond before it can trade, and the bond is slashed if peers prove fraud. A single raven of bad actors can still enter, but cloning thousands of identities means locking thousands of bonds, so the cost scales with the attack. Each deposit is sealed with a cipher commitment, so identities stay private while the bond is publicly verifiable, and the registry is no haven for sockpuppets: honest agents get their bond back, cheaters fund the victims.
